  • In a recent development, it’s a rare data point.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, shows four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a fresh batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

In a recent development, it’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its upcoming Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, shows four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

Industry observers note that but the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

Sources indicate that HMD took its first truck on November 2 and says it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler said Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

In a recent development, the company ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

According to recent reports, owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

According to recent reports, tesla introduced volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It claims the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

So we’re left with proxies. Tesla notes its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how significant that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

In a recent development, the order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that indicates whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

Sources indicate that I think the semi is going to be a big seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

The 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

Good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering.
  • Industry observers note that but at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.

Recent findings suggest that recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

Industry observers note that but at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

According to recent reports, “We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya stated. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”.

CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers. It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Industry observers note that twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort, a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.

“We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu mentioned. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”.

One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

“The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya noted. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”.

According to recent reports, according to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry said have changed everything.

“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry said.

According to recent reports, other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

“Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”.

Sources indicate that his team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

In a recent development, other inventions sought to get users off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

Industry observers note that “I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae said. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”.

In a recent development, also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.

“The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev noted. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”.

Industry observers note that his prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he prepares to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

Andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

Industry observers note that “We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards noted. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”.

Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:.

It has been revealed that this cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

To do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.

“We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat said. “Maybe even globally.”.

Industry News: Backed by Samsung, SK Hynix, and the Korean government, Rebellions CEO Sunghyun Park wants to prove sovereign AI pays off

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that few corporate rivalries are as fierce as the one between Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
  • Sources indicate that park’s organization sits at the center of government policy.
  • Rebellions may be the clearest test of whether sovereign AI can produce something more than an expensive also-ran.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that few corporate rivalries are as fierce as the one between Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The world’s leading manufacturer of memory chips and the world’s leading manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, respectively, are fighting for the title of South Korea’s most valuable company. In one area, though, the two are on the same team: Both back Rebellions, the $2.3 billion chip startup cofounded by Sunghyun Park—a veteran of Intel, SpaceX, and Morgan Stanley—that fronts South Korea’s push for sovereign silicon or AI chips that don’t depend on market leader Nvidia or any other U.S. or Chinese company.

Sources indicate that park’s organization sits at the center of government policy. “AI requires huge capital and huge talent,” he states. “Instead of having multiple players compete, the Korean government stated, ‘We need one champion. SK Hynix, please help him. Samsung, please help him. SK Telecom, KT’—top two data center companies—‘please become Rebellions’ customers.’”.

Rebellions may be the clearest test of whether sovereign AI can produce something more than an expensive also-ran. Korea is funneling its best resources toward Rebellions: Samsung’s foundries, SK Hynix’s memory, and government money. The Korea National Growth Fund co-led Rebellions’ $400 million round in March.

Will it pay off? Rebellions eventually wants public investors to back a risky bet on a chip startup in a market that—for now—is skeptical of AI stocks. Still, Park is hopeful. Rebellions’ backers make it “more powerful compared to any other player in the United States,” he notes. But market volatility and a wave of shelved data center IPOs will put his confidence to the test.

Park took the long road to national-champion-in-waiting. A graduate of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, he spent his compulsory military service in Afghanistan alongside the U.S. Army, where he learned English. Afterward, he earned a PhD in electrical engineering and computer science at MIT, and worked in chip engineering roles at Intel, SpaceX, and Morgan Stanley in the U.S. before returning to Korea to launch Rebellions.

Sources indicate that park and his cofounders—including Jinwook Oh, who designed AI chips at IBM, and Hyo-eun Kim, who developed deep-learning technology at a medical AI startup—founded Rebellions in 2020. It’s a “fabless” chip startup in that it handles only design and contracts manufacturing (or “fabrication”) out to a third party—in this case, Samsung.

In 2024, Rebellions merged with Sapeon, another chip designer backed by the SK Group. Samsung invested in the combined company in 2025.

Rebellions is part of a wave of startups challenging Nvidia by going after inference—what happens when someone uses ChatGPT, Claude, or DeepSeek—rather than training, which builds the models.

In a recent development, inference is “highly cost-sensitive,” claims Rakesh Kumar, a University of Illinois engineering professor and author of The Chip Age: How Semiconductors Became the World’s Most Powerful Resource. A $2 difference in price could be the reason someone chooses OpenAI over Anthropic.

Park, too, is pitching efficiency, rather than pure power. “From the hardware side, we claim only one metric,” he notes. “Tokens per second, per dollar, per watt.”.

Industry observers note that outside the U.S. and China—the clear leaders in the AI race—countries are trying to figure out how they can insulate themselves from the whims of foreign suppliers and governments.

It has been revealed that south Korea may take the idea most seriously. It has run a state-backed Korean-language-model competition since June 2025, and its “AI for All” initiative prepares to give Koreans free local chatbots. Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered AI counts only three countries with more than a handful of “notable AI models”: the U.S., with 59; China, with 35; and South Korea, with eight.

“Even my mom talks about sovereign AI, [and] she doesn’t know what sovereign AI is,” Park says.

“Elon didn’t just talk.” He went into the manufacturing side of things himself, Park claims of his ex-boss. “There are a lot of books on leadership, but the baseline is this: We need to work hard—whatever the role.”.

Recent findings suggest that the catch is that sovereign AI programs may lead to models and chips that are less capable, less efficient, and more costly than what comes out of the U.S. or China. Such startups can’t take advantage of the same economies of scale as established players and are selling their products to a smaller customer base. “You’re spending all this money with no guarantee of success,” Kumar says. Without Nvidia’s scale, “you might actually have higher costs.”.

Recent findings suggest that rebellions, which counts backers KT and SK Telecom as customers, hopes to list in Seoul next year, though Park says it will depend on market conditions. The government wants a Korean listing first—for “national security”—before a second listing abroad, he says.

Other AI IPOs have gone astray. At least three AI-related companies—Australia’s Firmus and AirTrunk, and SK Hynix’s U.S. unit Solidigm—suspended their IPOs in October, citing market uncertainty. Investors have also punished AI shares amid worries about high debt and massive capital expenditure.

According to recent reports, park is unfazed by market swings—perhaps a benefit of having the Korean government and the country’s two most valuable companies as backers. But he knows that AI firms will eventually have to prove they can turn a profit. He expects the judgment to come by 2029: “Then, the market will test whether these investments are paying off or not.”.

  • According to the data, XRP’s Supply Shortage Index on Binance has surged to 2.4 as of November 19 despite the asset’s extreme price weakness in recent days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The price of XRP has continued to slump to deeper levels amid the prolonged market volatility. However, recent onchain data has shown an unexpected trend in exchange activity.

According to the latest data from crypto analytics platform Cryptoquant, XRP is presently facing a severe supply shortage on the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance.

According to the data, XRP’s Supply Shortage Index on Binance has surged to 2.4 as of November 19 despite the asset’s extreme price weakness in recent days.

Notably, the data further shows that the metric has surpassed the previous reading of 2.09 recorded on July 6, marking a five-month high in XRP’s supply shortage index.

It is notable to note that readings above +2 are a strong indication of severely tightened supply, which means that the amount of XRP available on the exchange has decreased significantly.

While negative readings often mean the opposite, this means that XRP has witnessed a sharp reversal from the supply level seen on September 27.

At the time, the index stood at -1.5 while XRP traded above $1.50, signaling an abundance of XRP on Binance. This means that more tokens were available for trading during the period, which potentially added to selling pressure.

While that is no longer the case, the latest data shows that the XRP supply index has jumped by 3.9 points in just 53 days, moving from supply abundance to severe supply tightness in just about two months.

This typically suggests that XRP is being aggressively moved out of exchanges despite its prolonged price weakness, potentially driving a rebound in the demand for XRP, which could eventually trigger a price recovery.

Tech Report: Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk now says Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first unveiled it was killing it.
  • The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it notes about Tesla’s future as a company that sells cars to people.
  • Sources indicate that on November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk now says Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first unveiled it was killing it.

The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it notes about Tesla’s future as a company that sells cars to people.

Sources indicate that on November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.

In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027.

According to recent reports, the reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of initiative, Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers, and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program.

And the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.

According to recent reports, tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.

It has been revealed that some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.

Recent findings suggest that the most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”.

Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”.

According to recent reports, that’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t confirmed a single new consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that launched in 2017 and 2020.

Tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years.

Sources indicate that even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.

We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.

Recent findings suggest that the pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car aims for Robotaxi in 2024. No latest consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.

I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.

As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.

In a recent development, A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.

Recent findings suggest that tesla is becoming a firm that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.

The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On-chain data indicates the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.
  • It has been revealed that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT.
  • Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data indicates the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

It has been revealed that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

It has been revealed that blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

It has been revealed that if Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

In a recent development, the FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It highlights how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

In a recent development, binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

In a recent development, while the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now reveals:.

Recent findings suggest that the first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what consumers hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

In a recent development, why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

Sources indicate that the striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Industry observers note that compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance notes it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance notes the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am.
  • Many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week.
  • Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am.

Many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week. But not all the upcoming goodies confirmed there (or simultaneous with this year’s Microsoft Ignite show, which kicked off Nov. 17) might have made it onto everyone’s radar.

Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365. But there was some other vital news last week that Microsoft customers could find equally, if not more, interesting and useful.

Among my picks for the “make sure you didn’t miss this” list:.

Copilot without the M365 subscription prerequisite arrives next week: Despite a LOT of talk about Copilot, “a upcoming OS for work,” Microsoft didn’t mention anything at all during Ignite about a new purchasing option for Copilot that is set to go live on Dec. 1. Starting then, Microsoft will offer a version of Copilot to small business and enterprise customers without the current prerequisite of having a certain paid Microsoft 365 plan.

For a flat fee of $21 per user per month for small businesses and $30 per user per month for enterprise customers (before discounts), users will be able to buy this latest standalone Copilot offering, as Microsoft quietly announced back in October on its Partner Center site.

Currently, to buy Copilot, business customers need to have purchased a qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription strategy before they shell out even more money for Copilot. Because of this requirement, Microsoft isn’t competitive price-wise when pitted against OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude entry-level business tiers.

The latest offer is for new customers buying through any of Microsoft’s channels, including its Cloud Solution Provider program, across commercial, education, government and nonprofit sectors.

I’ve got a lot of questions about this fresh offer, including where Copilot chats are stored and how/if customers will get some kind of access to the Microsoft IQ technology that underlies Copilot and is positioned as its secret sauce if they don’t have a Microsoft 365 subscription. I’ve asked Microsoft, but no word back so far.

Azure Linux 4.0 is now ready for prime time: Announced on the same day Ignite kicked off (but without a mention during the conference), Microsoft’s own commercial Linux distribution, Azure Linux 4.0, is now generally available.

The 4.0 release is interesting for a few reasons. First, it is the first release of Azure Linux — formerly known as Common Base Linux (CBL)-Mariner — designed as a general-purpose server OS for customer virtual machines, and it is based on the Fedora Linux stack. Checking off the requisite AI box, Azure Linux 4.0 is “purpose-built for cloud native and AI workloads,” as Microsoft mentioned back in May.

Microsoft officials have remarked two-thirds of customer cores in Azure run Linux (not Windows Server). Microsoft has acknowledged the platforms running Microsoft 365, GitHub and OpenAI’s ChatGPT “all sit on Linux foundations.”.

Microsoft has supported a wide variety of Linux distributions on Azure for years but never made its own available for commercial use by customers and partners until now.

According to recent reports, windows Server 2028 is in the works: Yes, another on-premises version of Windows Server is coming. Christened Windows Server 2028, the next release, likely to debut in late 2027, is now in public preview.

Microsoft mentioned Server 2028 in its Book of News and in passing in some sessions, but it was not positioned as a top-tier announcement.

The 2028 release includes some expected and a few surprise features, such as making 32-bit app support an optional component rather than installing it by default. That change, along with a hardened Server Core configuration included by default, is designed to improve the security of the platform from the get-go. But they may present potential backward-compatibility risks.

It has been revealed that microsoft is positioning Server 2028 similarly to the way it has been pushing Windows client lately: as a way to run AI workloads more cheaply because they can run locally. The “unmetered intelligence” pitch strikes again.

Sure, Microsoft can’t make every announcement a centerpiece in a two-plus-hour (waah!) opening keynote. But sometimes, hidden gems deserve their moments in the sun. Or pouring rain ….

Bitcoin (BTC), the world’s largest cryptocurrency, is flashing a major, ‘scary’ technical signal that was absent even during its last major crashes in February and June 2026.

The flagship coin has crashed to a fresh 4.5-month low amid persistent institutional outflows totaling billions from cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

$BTC hasn't formed a higher high for 16 consecutive days now. This didn't even happen during the Feb 2026 and June 2026 crashes. https://t.co/I6IPmdueEc.

Bitcoin has failed to form a higher high for the past 16 days. This is a very long stretch, one that was absent during Bitcoin’s February and June crashes.

Recent findings suggest that A higher high, in the context of technical analysis, is formed when an asset’s price reaches a fresh high point above its previous swing high. The absence of higher highs signals that buyers are having a hard time taking back control of the market.

The latest Bitcoin price action adds further to concerns surrounding the future of the flagship cryptocurrency.

Earlier today, BTC crashed to $61,225, its lowest price point in around four and a half months.

Bitcoin's failure to create higher highs despite several attempts to recover shows that selling pressure remains quite high.

Nevertheless, this technical pattern of 16 days without a higher high does not necessarily spell more pain for Bitcoin. If the cryptocurrency can decisively push above recent resistance zones, it may be a sign that buyers are starting to make a comeback.

Bitcoin is facing persistent withdrawals of huge amounts of money from U.S.-based spot Bitcoin ETFs.

Recent findings suggest that blackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) witnessed its biggest-ever daily net outflow on Nov. 19.

Industry observers note that the crypto fund suffered a whopping $541.1 million in net withdrawals on the day. At the same time, total net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs amounted to around $582.3 million across the entire market.

Industry observers note that more alarmingly, the fresh wave of withdrawals brings cumulative net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs to around $3.47 billion so far this November.

The ETFs have seen negative net flows on 12 of the first 14 trading days of the month.

#99059. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1358 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1358 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • It has been revealed that most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves.
  • According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to newly introduced institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

It has been revealed that most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to newly introduced institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company claims R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery remarked the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

In a recent development, the model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

Recent findings suggest that the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as latest rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

According to recent reports, the risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

Sources indicate that the OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

It has been revealed that eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent manufacturer, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

Industry observers note that for everyday customers, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

Recent findings suggest that after opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD stated the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a newly introduced record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD stated the issue stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

The organization noted it “immediately” released an investigation and corrected the problem so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a new visual error-prevention mechanism to limit challenges like this going forward.

BYD said the issue does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

In a recent development, the company mentioned owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD mentioned, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

Industry observers note that all versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

In comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

According to recent reports, based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li noted the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:47 am.

SenseNet, a startup providing wildfire detection and intelligence, on Tuesday revealed a $43 million financing package. The Vancouver, B.C.-based company says the funding will support its expansion across the U.S. and internationally.

According to recent reports, the startup uses a suite of technologies for the rapid detection of wildfires, including environmental sensors, AI-enabled cameras, satellite data, drone technology and predictive analytics. Its monitoring footprint covers 450 million acres in a dozen countries.

SenseNet indicates its technology has provided early alerts for more than 10,000 fires, in some cases hours before the first 911 calls.

“Wildfire protection is no longer just about detecting a fire as quickly as possible. It’s about understanding what’s happening, what could happen next, and giving the right people the information they need to act,” Hamed Noori, co-founder and CEO of SenseNet, said in a statement.

According to recent reports, noori launched SenseNet in 2019 with Chief Technology Officer Shahab Bahrami. Both hold doctorates in electrical and computer engineering from the University of British Columbia.

The Series B round was led by Idealist Capital, with participation from Fusion Fund, Stormbreaker Ventures, Thin Line Capital, National Bank of Canada and The Sitka Foundation.

The financing includes purchases of newly issued shares, which put money into SenseNet; secondary share sales, which pay existing shareholders; and debt. SenseNet did not disclose how much of the $43 million falls into each category.

The startup previously raised $12.78 million and has 30 employees, according to PitchBook.

Sources indicate that senseNet competes with companies including OroraTech, Dryad and Pano AI, whose cameras, software and alerting services are used by Washington’s Department of Natural Resources to detect wildfires. The companies are developing their technology as warming temperatures and drier conditions increase wildfire risks.

Transaction activity declined afterward, and the decline intensified amid the sell-off that hit the market in recent weeks.

The latest figures suggest that fewer transactions are taking place across Shibarium compared with periods of stronger activity. The key question now is whether Shibarium can regain momentum in the coming weeks.

Meanwhile, development continues behind the scenes for the Shiba Inu layer-2 network, as long-time Shiba Inu community member and developer Mazrael revealed a big batch of contracts deployed on Puppynet, Shibarium's testnet.

But in the meantime, Shibarium’s fall to three-digit activity levels is a major slowdown that SHIB holders and ecosystem watchers will be watching closely.

Shiba Inu's on-chain holders increased as the number of wallets holding SHIB hit 1,700,930 on November 19, 2026.

According to the latest figures shared by Etherscan SHIB, an X account dedicated to providing updates on the SHIB ecosystem, the cryptocurrency added 236 latest on-chain holders in a single day, taking its total past the 1.7 million milestone.

The month of November has also seen consistent growth, with SHIB adding 4,520 holders since the start of the month. The broader 2026 trend is even more pronounced, with the number of holders of the token increasing by 152,300 since the beginning of the year.

While Shiba Inu's latest milestone seems remarkable, Mazrael suggested that the Shib ecosystem, including Shibarium, might have more holders than indicated, with 1.4 million holders of Binance-pegged SHIB on the BNB Chain.

According to recent reports, "Shibarium has more holders than those you listed, though. But yeah. Well, there are also 1.4 million holders of Binance-pegged SHIB on BNB. But that's not actually CCIP SHIB; it is a peg," Mazrael wrote.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A large organization was preparing to move a group of customer-service teams onto a upcoming order-management platform.
  • The issue hadn’t caused a failed launch checkpoint, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large organization was preparing to move a group of customer-service teams onto a upcoming order-management platform. Two weeks before the first wave, the program director saw a pattern in the integration testing: Orders were still processing, but the time between the customer system and the back-end platform was getting less predictable.

The issue hadn’t caused a failed launch checkpoint, though.

The program director escalated it anyway because resolving it might require the technology team to redirect shared engineering capacity from another priority.

The senior team reviewed the issue and returned it for monitoring because there were more immediate launch risks on the table, and this one had no confirmed business impact yet. The program director kept it visible inside the program, but the engineers who could change the shared capacity remained committed elsewhere.

Nine days later, the same integration delay began appearing often enough to disrupt final practice sessions.

Training teams had to repeat exercises, supervisors lost preparation time, and the technology team had to pull engineers back into work that could have been addressed earlier with more room to move.

By the time the integration problem returned to senior attention, the program had fewer choices.

The delay itself had started consuming time across the rollout. Practice sessions had to be repeated when response times changed from one exercise to the next, and technology specialists were pulled into additional troubleshooting calls to determine whether the variation came from the integration or normal test activity.

Program leaders were now coordinating repeated work across training and technology while the launch window kept narrowing. That repeated work also displaced other readiness activity for the same rollout wave.

Technology specialists who were rechecking integration behavior had less time for remaining validation tasks, while program leads spent more of the day coordinating exceptions instead of closing other open launch items.

Sources indicate that the issue was now consuming capacity meant for other launch work. The issue also consumed senior attention at a worse moment.

Earlier, the decision had been whether to free a small amount of shared engineering capacity to investigate a developing risk. Now the decision included training disruption, launch timing and the impact of taking engineers away from other committed work.

The problem hadn’t appeared “suddenly.” The fact is that the cost had grown while the issue sat below the level where the cross-functional authority to change the resource commitment existed.

After the first wave, leadership asked teams to raise developing issues sooner. The program added earlier warning triggers around integration stability and asked workstream leads to bring forward concerns before they threatened a formal milestone.

That response improved detection.

The next rollout wave produced more early warnings, including smaller variations in system response that would previously have stayed inside the testing team.

It has been revealed that the same integration issue also remained under observation. Whenever the delay moved outside its expected range, the program director raised it sooner rather than waiting for the pattern to become persistent.

It has been revealed that the volume of developing issues now reaching the senior team was higher. Some required action immediately. Others, including the integration concern, still depended on how the pattern developed over several days.

The senior team had to sort them.

Industry observers note that the strongest challenges stayed active because their impact was already clear. A confirmed system defect, a missed supplier commitment or a customer-facing problem was easier to keep in the senior discussion because the consequence was visible.

Industry observers note that the integration glitch sat in a harder category. It had been raised early, but the team still couldn’t say whether the delay would stabilize, worsen or stay within the range the launch could absorb.

So, the senior team returned it for continued monitoring while keeping attention on issues with clearer impact.

That’s where the “Hidden Problems” leak appears. The issue was surfaced, understood and still lost senior visibility before the organization had enough evidence to treat it as urgent.

In a recent development, some developing problems belong below the senior team. Local leaders should solve them when the work, resources and authority sit within their control.

This concern didn’t fit that pattern.

The testing team could observe the integration delay, and the program director could adjust local sequencing, but neither could move engineering capacity from another enterprise priority.

Recent findings suggest that that distinction matters because earlier escalation only helps when the issue remains visible at a level with enough authority to act on it. If the issue is sent back to a level that can watch but can’t remove the constraint, the organization has improved detection without improving its ability to respond while options are still open.

Sources indicate that in the next rollout wave, the same pattern became easier to see earlier. That didn’t mean it became easier to carry in the senior discussion.

Leadership responded to the first wave by adding earlier indicators. That made the program better at finding developing problems before they became formal failures. It also increased the number of challenges competing for the same senior attention.

As more concerns arrived earlier, triage became stricter. Challenges with immediate consequences stayed active. Developing issues with uncertain timing or impact were more likely to be returned for monitoring until the picture became clearer.

The integration problem therefore moved through the same cycle again. It was raised sooner, reviewed sooner and returned sooner. Earlier detection improved while the amount of senior attention available to carry every developing issue forward stayed fixed.

Recent findings suggest that the response had strengthened one part of the system and exposed the limit in another. More early warnings entered the senior layer, but the organization still had to decide which ones remained there.

The usual question is whether teams are escalating early enough, and in this case, they were.

Recent findings suggest that the harder test is what happens after a developing issue reaches senior attention while it’s still uncertain. If it requires cross-functional authority, shared resources or a choice that local leaders can’t make, returning it for monitoring leaves the need for senior action unresolved. It delays the point at which that action becomes unavoidable.

By then, the issue usually carries more consequence and fewer options.

It has been revealed that the company improved the speed of detection after the first rollout wave. What it hadn’t changed was the amount of leadership attention available to keep unresolved, developing issues active before their cost became obvious.

Earlier escalation works only when the organization can keep the right uncertain problems visible long enough to act before they become urgent.

Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano is facing fresh criticism for struggling to attract customers and generate on-chain activity, despite being nearly nine years into its development.

Widely-followed crypto analyst Lark Davis has branded the network a “largely failed blockchain,” pointing to a stark adoption gap with Solana, which released four years later but has significantly outpaced ADA in daily users, perpetual futures trading volume, and application revenue.

It has been revealed that despite having nearly a decade to establish itself in the blockchain industry, Cardano continues to face questions about its ability to attract consumers and generate meaningful network activity. Analyst Lark Davis has commented on the adoption gap between Cardano and Solana, arguing that Solana has significantly outperformed ADA despite launching four years later.

“Nine years in and Cardano is still waiting on adoption,” Davis wrote on X.

According to Davis, Cardano accounts for just around 1% of Solana’s daily people, highlighting the stark difference in activity between the two networks. The gap reportedly extends beyond user numbers, with Cardano recording only about 0.3% of Solana’s perpetual futures trading volume.

The revenue figures paint an even more challenging picture for the Cardano ecosystem. Davis estimates that Cardano generates roughly 0.2% of the application revenue recorded across Solana’s ecosystem, further highlighting the difference in economic activity between the competing networks.

Based on these figures, Davis delivered a particularly harsh assessment of Cardano, describing it as a “largely failed blockchain.” His criticism centers on the contrast between Cardano’s nine-year journey and Solana’s ability to build a considerably larger user base and generate more trading activity and application revenue in a shorter period.

It has been revealed that the latest criticism follows a series of similar remarks from Davis about Cardano’s adoption challenges. As ZyCrypto previously reported, the analyst had also taken aim at Cardano over its relatively small user base, questioning the network’s ability to attract and retain users despite years of development.

Despite his harsh assessment of Cardano’s fundamentals, Davis has occasionally expressed optimism about ADA’s price prospects.

In November 2025, for instance, he suggested that Cardano could stage a rally similar to XRP’s 2024 surge, pointing to the strength of its community and brand as potential catalysts.

More recently, on September 28, Davis argued that Cardano’s “cult following” could help drive ADA back toward $1, with further upside potentially taking the token to $1.50 or even $2.

However, these bullish price projections focused more on speculative market demand and Cardano’s dedicated community than on measurable improvements in network adoption or ecosystem activity.

#99053. Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time

Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm.
  • Industry observers note that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Sources indicate that when startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm.

Industry observers note that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Sources indicate that when startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models. He got in touch with urban planners at Bellevue City Hall, and together they combed through nearly 300 land use permit applications to find common mistakes and bottlenecks.

It has been revealed that bellevue began using Rabah’s platform, Govstream.AI, in the summer of 2025, starting with an AI assistant for city staff. In a test using past applications, about three times as many were judged complete with Govstream’s tool. Rabah says that change alone has the potential to alter the housing stock of the city.

“Why can’t we build more housing? All the macro economic reasons, inflation, material costs, labor, land scarcity, are all exacerbated by the slow permitting process,” Rabah said. “That’s what we want to change.”.

So, how did Rabah, a B2B software engineer by training, find his way to land use permitting?

Industry observers note that rabah hadn’t heard of the government technology sector, aka GovTech, until mid-career, but looking back, the signs were all there. He was born in Sfax, Tunisia, and grew up in Tunis. Throughout his childhood, he dreamed of running for office.

According to recent reports, “I come from a small developing country, so there’s always this idea of, what could a small developing country become? How can it prosper and grow?” Rabah said. “Building has always been a significant part of what I imagined myself doing.”.

It has been revealed that as a teenager in the 1980s, he attended a USAID-funded boarding school in Tunis. The school was part of Cold War efforts to expand American soft power around the Middle East; classes were conducted in English and many of the students went on to university in North America.

Industry observers note that “The school had the first Macintosh lab in all of Africa,” Rabah remarked. “I can still picture the USAID logo on the back of each computer.”.

Rabah got a scholarship to University of British Columbia, where he studied electrical engineering while running what he calls his “first entrepreneurial venture”: a service that built and hosted websites for small businesses.

That led to a job at a startup called Pivotal, a customer relationship management platform where Rabah led a team responsible for e-business applications. After Pivotal went public, Rabah left for a job at TELUS, one of Canada’s “substantial three” telecommunications corporations, but swiftly felt frustrated by the dynamics at such a large company.

It has been revealed that “Even though I worked on nascent products, it was very, very bureaucratic,” Rabah remarked. “There were committees, a hundred thousand employees. I missed building things.”.

Rabah began to look for a newly introduced job that would not only allow him to build but also to make a difference.

“Being an immigrant, it’s always tempting to stay content with having a good job, good status,” Rabah noted. “But I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”.

That vision led him to Socrata, which in 2010 was just a nascent government technology startup.

It has been revealed that “I really connected with the founder,” Rabah said. “It had a really cool mission, it combined the ‘do-well’ with ‘do-good.’”.

According to recent reports, socrata was one of the first platforms to host data portals for local governments and federal agencies, allowing citizens to access and map public data sets. Many U.S. cities, including Seattle, still use Socrata’s software today to publish information including crime logs, permits, and budgets.

“We were a big part of pioneering the open data movement,” Rabah said. “At one point almost every major city was our customer, and half the states.”.

Socrata was acquired by Tyler Technologies in 2018, and Rabah stayed on until 2024.

According to recent reports, “The funny part is today we use that data quite a lot in our work because one of the most popular data sets that any city publishes is its permit data,” Rabah mentioned. “We’ve even built a connector between Socrata and Govstream.”.

But once Socrata was acquired, Rabah began to feel the same way he had at TELUS: boxed in by bureaucracy.

According to recent reports, “Tyler was a really good tech giant, but it is a massive company,” Rabah said. “Tech was getting repetitive, and I was thinking about leaving it altogether.”.

“The thing that pushed me over the edge is that AI happened,” Rabah noted. “It was one of those moments where once you start working with it, you really can’t help but think, ‘I can revisit virtually every assumption I’ve made over the last 20 years, every constraint.’”.

Immediately, he thought of his passion for building—building a startup, building a better country, and literally building a building.

In a recent development, “I’ve been fascinated by the built environment since my Lego days: What makes some cities livable and others not?” Rabah noted. “Then, living in Seattle, you see the lack of housing, affordability, and the homelessness problem we have, and you’re like, why can’t we build more housing? I started believing that these problems are in fact solvable if we simply speed things up and simplify things with AI.”.

In July of 2024, Rabah began working with his “design partner,” Bellevue’s Development Services Department, to learn more about common permitting problems.

According to recent reports, “We started with something visionary and high-level, but you can only get there if you understand the granular problems of the day-to-day,” Rabah said. “So we talked with developers and builders and we talked with the people on the other side of the counter who are processing these permits and guiding these builders.”.

He learned that most permitting mistakes are avoidable, like applying for the wrong zone or forgetting to include a north arrow on an architectural proposal. Those oversights can send an application back to square one while clogging up the permitting process for all other projects.

“The wait time disproportionately affects lower margin projects,” Rabah said. “It really constrains the supply of housing, especially the housing we need more of, which is the more affordable kind.”.

Govstream’s AI assistants are designed to help first-time builders avoid those errors and make permitting faster for everyone. Rabah and his team began by building what they call an “intelligent intake” platform for a city permitting portal, which guided owners through preparing to submit their applications.

When Bellevue first tested Govstream’s intake tool on 276 past residential building permit applications, the city reported a completeness rate of 67%, compared with 22% when those applications were originally filed. According to the tech giant, the latest testing has yielded an 88% completeness rate.

More recently, they’ve begun to build out an AI assistant for the backend, which assists city permit techs with the initial review and reduces what Rabah calls “toil,” like answering unnecessary pre-application emails and tracking down missing documents.

Bellevue staff estimated that Govstream’s tools saved them 152 hours over one month this summer by helping them research and respond to pre-application inquiries.

It has been revealed that “For a developer, time is money, so the type of housing that can be built in Bellevue will become more affordable,” said Jake Hesselgesser, Bellevue’s development services director. “This technology has a direct and material impact on the cost of housing.”.

Eventually, Govstream.AI will be an end-to-end service, assisting in later stages of the permitting process, too. But Rabah is emphatic that Govstream will not give AI the final say.

“We always put our AI systems in the role of assistants that suggest stuff, but never decide stuff,” Rabah noted.

Rabah claims Govstream uses preset rules, outside the AI model, to check whether a portion of the application is complete, whether a site needs a geotechnical report, or whether an architect is properly licensed. In Bellevue, city staff retain final authority.

Hesselgesser mentioned that Rabah’s conservative approach to AI is what made the city of Bellevue want to work with his startup.

“Our core principle around Bellevue’s use of AI is to retain human decision making, and we wanted to ensure that we were aligned with a firm with the same core value,” Hesselgesser said. “Saf took that holistic approach.”.

Around the office, Rabah has become known for his eagerness to build. According to Mariia Derevianko, head of marketing, he spends his weekends building out a product or an idea in order to workshop it with the team.

In a recent development, “He’s very hands-on with the product, with design, marketing, all of the aspects,” Derevianko mentioned. “He never waits for the engineers to build something.”.

Most recently, he built a lead tracker to research which cities Govstream should partner with, and previously, he vibe-coded one of the research assistants in the Govstream platform as a template for his software engineers.

Derevianko, who joined the team last year after Rabah poached her from AWS, said he’s also known for his kindness.

It has been revealed that “I originally didn’t want to join a start-up,” Derevianko stated. “I only said yes because I saw he is a genuinely good person who really cares about this project.”.

Govstream.AI has already won at least 12 contracts around the Puget Sound, including King County and the City of Everett, as well as cities across the country, such as Louisville, Kentucky.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, Rabah has his eyes set on Seattle, where construction and development has been on the decline. Last December, the city council passed permanent “middle housing” rules to upzone residential neighborhoods and encourage the construction of ADUs, all of which will need a permit.

In a recent development, seattle tested a competing AI tool from CivCheck in 2025. In June, city staff recommended a pilot that would let applicants check their submissions for completeness before filing.

Industry observers note that “We need affordable housing in Seattle,” Rabah noted. “We would really, really love to help our home city streamline permitting and remove it as a barrier.”.

In founding Govstream.AI, Rabah has found the job he has been looking for: one in which he can build things without the bureaucracy of a large manufacturer, all while “doing good.”.

“This has become my obsession,” Rabah said. “I can point to things in a city and say, maybe Govstream was a part of what allowed this project to get built.”.

NEAR Protocol (NEAR) fell 11.41% on Nov. 20 and traded at $2.84, according to TradingView data. In early October, the token was trading near $6, and it has lost about half of its value since then.

It has been revealed that over the same period, the volume of NEAR Intents went up. "NEAR went from $6 to $3 in about a month. funny thing is, NEAR Intents is doing more volume now than it did in october," NEAR ecosystem contributor Evgeny Haenko wrote on X on Nov. 20.

According to Haenko, NEAR Intents averaged around $129 million in daily volume in October, and in November it was processing around $134 million a day. "The price got cut in half, the business didn't slow down at all. hard for me to be bearish here," he wrote.

NEAR Intents lets people swap assets across more than 30 blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and XRP. The service is built into wallets such as Ledger, Trust Wallet and Brave. Over the past year, its trading volume grew 7.1 times to $39.5 billion.

Sources indicate that NEAR Intents has collected about $63 million in fees in total, and the network keeps about 29% of that amount. Fees on the NEAR Intents interface, payments from B2B partners and the spread on better-than-market trades accounted for 16.3%, 9.9% and 2.8% of the fees, respectively. Over the last 30 days, the protocol earned about $1.8 million, compared with $2.2 million in October.

Industry observers note that since February 2026, the protocol has used NEAR Intents revenue to buy NEAR on the market. More than 1.84 million NEAR have gone to the buyback wallet so far, and that is 41.6% of all distributed onchain revenue. Base transaction fees on the network are burned in full.

Recent findings suggest that in early November, the NEAR community also voted to cut the maximum annual issuance from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years. The proposal, HSP-029, went through House of Stake, NEAR's governance initiative, and Haenko is one of its participants.

Industry observers note that on Sept. 29, Bitwise released the first U.S. spot NEAR ETF on NYSE Arca under the ticker NRR. Two days later, on Oct. 1, NEAR Intents paused its services after an exploit that cost about $3.8 million, and the team promised to compensate people in full. The exploiter later returned the funds. "The funds from the $3.8M NEAR Intents hack were sent back in full," NEAR Intents general manager Alex Shevchenko remarked at the time.

💡 Key Takeaways
