  • In a recent development, bell was used to the sound of her three kids running around, watching cartoons and eating Pop-Tarts.
  • In a recent development, her ex-husband had taken action while she was trying to make sense of what had happened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After her divorce, Hannah Hembree Bell found herself sitting alone at home on a Saturday night in a house that was too quiet.

In a recent development, bell was used to the sound of her three kids running around, watching cartoons and eating Pop-Tarts. By the time her divorce was finalized, her kids didn’t live with her, and she paid child support.

In a recent development, her ex-husband had taken action while she was trying to make sense of what had happened. He reached out to their shared friends first and consulted so many lawyers that it was hard for Bell to find one to represent her.

The first Saturday after the split, Bell gripped the edges of her bathroom’s countertop, stared at herself in the mirror and sobbed until she could hardly recognize her own face. She didn’t know if she could keep going.

Then, out of the corner of her eye, she saw a faded Post-It note she had stuck up years earlier. It encouraged her to wait; courage and strength would come. In that moment, she decided that her life was not over.

“I’m going to choose to be better, not bitter,” she recalls thinking at the time.

In a recent development, bell was in law school at the time. Her path into the legal world arrived through business school. While earning an online MBA from Liberty University, she took a business law class taught by a practicing attorney. She realized her brain lit up when she read case law and tried to argue both sides in her head.

Industry observers note that one day, she read an opinion and predicted what the judge would do. She was right. It was the first time she considered law as a career. She was turning 30 years old at the time and wondered if she could pull off pursuing a law career while also raising her children. She decided to give it a shot.

Her first day of law school in 2012 was also her oldest daughter’s first day of kindergarten. Bell went to Saint Mary’s University School of Law and eventually graduated summa cum laude.

As she was commuting an hour and 20 minutes each way to the St. Mary’s campus, Bell’s marriage unraveled. Like many women she now represents, she poured all of her emotional resources into staying in the marriage, not planning for what leaving would actually look like.

“I had not done anything in terms of planning or getting ready to get divorced or getting strategically prepared,” she says.

When she finally filed for divorce in 2014, she assumed her three children would simply move with her and see their dad every other weekend; she “did not foresee the world” in which that didn’t happen.

Recent findings suggest that her ex-husband saw things differently. “I was caught very surprised when he was like, ‘Oh no, you’re not taking these kids… You can leave, but they’re not going,’” she recalls.

Bell shares that entering her divorce unprepared, without a plan or organized finances, cost her custody of her three children and led to her paying child support. Her husband had primary custody. Bell only saw her children every other weekend and on Tuesday nights for an hour and 15 minutes. The divorce outcome plunged Bell into the “lowest moment” of her life. She went from running a busy house to sitting alone in a silent home most nights.

“I had to rebuild my entire identity, my entire everything really, from the bottom,” she indicates.

It has been revealed that at the same time, she was still attending law school. She describes herself in that period as “wrung out” emotionally. She spent everything she had on trying to save the marriage before the legal process even began.

Sources indicate that “It was too much in hindsight; it’s too much for one person to be trying to deal with and handle,” she states. She now urges women to take six months to prepare strategically before filing for divorce if they can. Her own lack of planning was her biggest mistake.

Years later, after a grueling custody modification process, Bell’s children ended up primarily living with her. However, she never forgot how unprepared and alone she felt in the early years.

Bell’s own family law odyssey eventually collided with her law career. After graduating from St. Mary’s, she spent two years at a large firm doing employment work. However, the experience of navigating a divorce showed her just how brutal and confusing the system could be, even for a lawyer.

On a WiFi-less flight to visit the man who would become her second husband, Drew, she started sketching numbers on a scrap of paper, wondering if she could make a small family law practice work. She came up with the idea for Hembree Bell Law on the back of a napkin.

Industry observers note that with no savings to fall back on, Bell asked Drew for a $10,000 loan. It was just enough to cover two months of her take-home pay so she could quit her job and launch. He agreed, and Bell started the law firm.

It has been revealed that bell went full-time with Hembree Bell Law in 2018, initially growing through referrals and networking. She turned posts into videos and layered in paid search and more sophisticated campaigns as the firm grew.

“Nothing will grow you faster than starting your own business and sticking with it,” she notes. “It takes a lot of grit, a lot of courage.”.

Along the way, she kept returning to the three mistakes she believes nearly cost her everything: not being prepared, not taking time to grieve and heal, and staying stuck in shame for too long.

Those themes became the backbone of a “My Confident Divorce” prep course she created to help women get ready before they file for divorce, so they don’t lose their “kids, money and sanity” the way she nearly did. “I really need to be the lawyer I wish I had had from the beginning,” she says.

Bell created the My Confident Divorce Law Firm last year. She designed the firm from the ground up for women who want more guidance and flexibility than a traditional law firm typically offers.

She pairs legal work with a concierge, mindset calls, community and AI to deliver a “coaching meets divorce” experience.

According to recent reports, while Hembree Bell Law is more of a conventional litigation firm, My Confident Divorce helps women initiative strategically for divorce months before filing documents. The firm tracks everything from parenting patterns to financial realities so that when the time comes, they can prove what matters in court.

Bell pulled in seven figures in revenue through her two firms last year and is aiming for eight figures this year.

In a recent development, “I feel like it’s my destiny to go back and help people not make the same mistakes that I made,” she says. “We help people end their marriage well.”.

#99049. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1297 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • The most vital words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

The most vital words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division remarked it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

According to recent reports, the staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

Sources indicate that that phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

Recent findings suggest that this is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

Sources indicate that the second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to customers.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the concerns presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

Industry observers note that the framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation claims what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

Recent findings suggest that the practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

  • The Seattle startup has debuted Zin Power, a new division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:58 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:58 am.

Sources indicate that zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats. But most of its business is now coming from what’s under the floor.

The Seattle startup has debuted Zin Power, a new division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.

The company also raised $5 million to scale up production and expanded its headquarters in the Interbay neighborhood to 11,000 square feet.

Sources indicate that about 90% of the tech giant’s revenue comes from selling motors and batteries to customers in the marine and drone industries, founder and CEO Piotr Zin told GeekWire. A typical setup includes two motors and about 500 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.

“We noticed a steady demand for pleasure craft year over year, but at the same time a massive increase in propulsion sales,” Zin noted.

Recent findings suggest that customers include StanCraft Wooden Boats, which teamed with Zin on the 340 Hammerhead E, an all-electric wooden runabout. StanCraft delivered the first one to a customer this summer.

Sources indicate that geekWire first checked out the firm in early 2024, when it was relaunching after a pandemic shutdown with its Z2R, a 20-foot carbon fiber runabout. Later that year Zin highlighted off the Z11, a 37-foot electric tender designed to shuttle passengers to and from megayachts at more than 60 mph. The company stated boats on the platform would cost $1.75 million to $3.75 million.

Sources indicate that the organization also offers the Z7 Convertible, a 22-foot runabout with a removable roof that it pitches for fishing, surfing and cruising. The boat has a top speed of 40 mph and a range of more than 80 miles.

It has been revealed that zin Power grew out of the drivetrains engineered for those boats. Zin sees the marine track record as a selling point for other industries that need high torque, including construction, mining and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).

“The ocean is one of the harshest environments there is, so the technology has already proven itself under about the toughest conditions it could face,” Zin noted.

In a recent development, many of those machines still run on diesel engines, a technology more than a century old. Zin said operators are eager to switch to electric.

“What’s interesting is that economics is driving the shift, not regulation or image,” he said.

Electric systems cost up to 70% less to operate, according to Zin. He estimated that replacing a single 250-horsepower industrial diesel engine that runs eight hours a day could save as much as $1.5 million over 10 years.

The latest funding will pay for more manufacturing capacity, a dedicated sales and engineering team to work with boat builders, and support for customers converting from diesel. Zin calls it a seed round, with a larger raise planned down the road. The company has raised $6.5 million to date, including a $1.275 million seed round in early 2024.

Zin Boats has nine full-time employees and brings on about a dozen contractors as needed.

For now, each Zin Power system is built to order. The company’s motors range from 100 to 600 kilowatts and deliver up to 2,700 pound-feet of torque, and its systems can run fully electric or as hybrids. A proprietary control unit that Zin Power calls the “Magic Box” manages everything from charging and cooling to software and safety.

“Our goal is to keep delivering what we’ve built while developing simpler, more advanced plug-and-play systems,” Zin said. “Eventually, we want a customer to be able to pull out a diesel engine and drop in a Zin Power system as a direct one-for-one replacement.”.

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

The award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 upcoming models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

It has been revealed that the judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

It has been revealed that kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

Industry observers note that it’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, introduced in May, outperformed the upcoming Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Sadly, Kia has no looks to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”.

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano-linked privacy blockchain Midnight has inked a major initial deal with a Japanese payments organization as it aims to make further inroads into traditional finance.

The news comes soon after a key breakthrough for Midnight in the United Kingdom, where Monument Bank started tokenizing customer deposits on the blockchain.

It has been revealed that per a Nov. 19 NADA NEWS report, Midnight Foundation President Fahmi Syed mentioned the foundation had inked an MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a major Japanese payments organization.

Sources indicate that syed did not name the manufacturer. But the deal is a big one for Midnight’s bid to establish a presence in Japan’s financial services sector.

However, it is just an initial agreement, and no commercial services have been rolled out in Japan yet.

It is also worth noting that the Midnight Foundation is talking to some major Japanese banks and companies working with intellectual property and medical data.

According to Syed, he spent two days in Tokyo meeting with major financial institutions and other companies.

Japan has been a key market for Midnight, along with the United States.

According to Midnight Foundation Japan country manager Taro Kimura, Japan is the only Asian country where the foundation has a local representative on the ground.

Midnight has been eyeing Japan more keenly due to the country’s sizeable Cardano community.

The Japanese push comes hot on the heels of a historic development in the British banking sector.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 18, British financial institution Monument Bank started tokenizing retail customer deposits on Midnight. It is the first UK bank to launch such a product on a public blockchain.

Recent findings suggest that the first phase of the venture involves up to £250 million in tokenized deposits. For this, the bank is offering customers a 12-month fixed annual interest rate of 5.2%.

Midnight employs zero-knowledge cryptography to safeguard sensitive transaction details, unlike traditional public blockchains. As a result, banks can meet compliance requirements while keeping their customers’ private information and transaction details out of public view.

BYD’s new EV may be about the size of a Toyota Camry, but it’s playing in a whole different league when it comes to technology.

BYD released the second-generation Seal 07 last week, calling it “the new choice for a class-leading luxury experience.”.

It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry.

Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology.

The newly introduced Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes.

The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its latest Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System.

Industry observers note that the setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System.

Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above.

BYD said the system provides ultra-fast response times down to the millisecond. The advanced suspension system adjusts damping force across a wide range of 100 to 10,000 Nm.

Recent findings suggest that it’s equipped on the all-electric Flagship Seal 07 variant, while lower-priced versions have the Disus-C intelligent body control system. The top-spec EV model with the Disus-M setup starts at 172,900 yuan ($26,000). Still, not too bad for what you get.

Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s new interior design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.

BYD added a few premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio.

Industry observers note that quite impressive for sure. What's more impressive is that GM/Cadillac first offered magnetic ride control back in 2002 (a full 24 years ago!!). It may not have been quite as advanced as this system in 2026, but still one of the most advanced suspension systems offered to date for a line of vehicles.

I really want this car!! I truly hope BYD will be able to sell this in the USA soon.

The Seal 07 also debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that lets drivers interact with the vehicle and manage functions remotely.

Higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super trade-in price” special, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

Living Computers closed, but its spirit and vintage machines live on at a museum south of Seattle

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 11:08 amNovember 24, 2026 at 11:09 am.
  • When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.
  • But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 11:08 amNovember 24, 2026 at 11:09 am.

When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.

But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.

It has been revealed that the Interim Computer Museum is a nonprofit that opened to the public in 2024 and has quietly grown into a hands-on showcase of dozens of machines, from early Apples and IBM PCs to hulking DEC systems that once filled university labs. At 4,400 square feet of public space, it’s nearly as significant as Living Computers was before that museum expanded in 2016.

ICM is led by Stephen Jones, who calls himself the museum’s “caretaker.” Jones spent two decades helping track down and restore machines for Allen, first at PDP Planet, Allen’s private collection of vintage systems, then at Living Computers, where he was senior engineering manager.

When the late Microsoft co-founder’s estate wound down Living Computers, the majority of the collection went to the Mimms Museum of Technology and Art in Georgia, where Jones is also a curator. The machines in Tukwila are privately owned, and Jones has helped bankroll ICM with personal funds, with plans to eventually donate the collection to the nonprofit.

He chose not to reuse the Living Computers name, which ICM now holds, because “it has a finite past.” Instead, he wants to carry on “the spirit of the engineering focus.”.

“Between Mimms and here, this is the legacy,” Jones mentioned. “We show the name and the connection to the past, but we’re doing newly introduced things.”.

ICM occupies space in Seattle Exchange @ Southcenter, a sprawl of low-slung flex buildings off Strander Boulevard near Westfield Southcenter mall. Its neighbors include a car detailer, a pest control company, a welding shop, an embroiderer and an upholsterer.

More than four decades ago, Seattle Computer Products operated just down Industry Drive. That’s where Tim Paterson wrote 86-DOS, the operating system Microsoft bought and turned into MS-DOS for IBM’s first PC.

Jones calls that proximity part of the “magic” of the location. The museum has a Gazelle computer that SCP built nearby, using boards that Jones said the manufacturer hired high school students to assemble and test. Volunteers recently pulled data off its hard drive, which boots into MS-DOS 2.11 and still holds SCP’s own source code.

It has been revealed that allen’s fingerprints are everywhere. One display holds a 1971 letter from Hellmut Golde, director of the University of Washington’s Computer Science Laboratory, kicking Allen and his “friends from the Lakeside School” out of the lab. Among the offenses: tying up the teletypes to print “endless listings,” and taking an acoustic coupler from a professor’s office “without leaving at least a note.” Golde asked them to turn in their keys.

The letter sits beside an Imlac PDS-1, the same type of graphics computer Golde scolded the teens for using without permission. More than five decades later, the letter is headed back to campus: ICM intends to display it, along with the Imlac, at UW’s 60th anniversary celebration for its computer science program in March.

In a recent development, jones recalled that Allen insisted visitors to Living Computers get “the 10-minute experience” of loading an Altair 8800 from paper tape, just as he remembered it. The kit computer was the machine for which Allen and Bill Gates wrote Microsoft’s first product, and Allen wanted to reinforce “how far we’ve come and how difficult old computers were.” ICM has an Altair 8800 on display.

Recent findings suggest that around the corner is Miss Piggy, a DEC datasystem 570 that Microsoft used in the early 1980s to support the group that built Multiplan, Word and later Excel. It was also the email host for much of the company, including Gates, who once had to print out an vital message on its console printer when the system went down before a speaking engagement.

According to recent reports, recovered email indicates Allen pushing to get Piggy networked. “Paul Allen is very keen on doing this,” Henry Burgess wrote in 1982. Retired in 1986, the machine now runs again in Tukwila. It’s one of ICM’s most popular remote systems, and some fans come in just to write programs while sitting next to it.

Other local ties include a PDP-7 that Boeing used to process flight data in the 1960s, and a Toad-1, a modern take on the PDP-10 built in the 1990s by Redmond’s XKL. Jones first got involved with Allen’s world through a 1997 Usenet post inviting PDP-10 enthusiasts onto a Toad. That machine became the cornerstone of PDP Planet.

In a 2024 video for Christie’s, Jones mentioned what inspired Allen was “being able to recover old programs, mythical code, and get them running on hardware so that they can be studied.”.

Sources indicate that asked what Allen would make of ICM, Jones didn’t hesitate. “I think he’d be happy,” he mentioned.

On a monitor beside ICM’s PDP-6, a 1968 artificial intelligence program is having trouble.

“SORRY, I DON’T KNOW THE WORD ‘STEEPLE,'” it replies.

The program is SHRDLU, created by Terry Winograd at the MIT AI Lab. It let a user type plain-English commands to move blocks around a virtual world. Only the PDP-6’s front console and display survived, so ICM is rebuilding the machine as a “hybrid,” with the original hardware wired to an emulator.

In a recent development, jones sees a lesson in that old error message. “You look at this and you think of how we use ChatGPT now,” he said. “The cool thing about SHRDLU is that it can tell you ‘I don’t know.’ It doesn’t try to fabricate anything.”.

ICM has its own ties to the modern AI world. An Anthropic employee is a member and strong supporter, and in October the museum brought six vintage computing stations to an Anthropic event, where the organization’s Claude chatbot wrote programs for machines like the Commodore 64.

Industry observers note that back in Tukwila, Claude has become one of ICM’s most useful restoration tools. The team feeds it huge stacks of scanned documentation, such as the full set of schematics for a PDP-10. When a machine has a logic fault, they ask where to look, and Claude points them to a page in the maintenance manual or a likely bad module.

“That’s turned things that would take a couple of weeks to solve into a couple of days,” Jones remarked.

It has been revealed that AI can point the way, but the repairs remain hands-on work. When Miss Piggy wouldn’t run properly this year, former Living Computers engineer Josh Dersch stepped through the machine’s microcode one instruction at a time using a recreated DEC test board, until he found a single bad chip. A spare board brought it back.

Asked if it still takes a human to keep these machines running, Jones agreed — at least for now. If a humanoid robot with AI built in ever indicates up to do the repairs, he joked, “then I sit at the front desk all day.”.

Nearly everything at ICM is meant to be touched, switched on and played with, and that can be intimidating. On machines with nothing but a text prompt, “you kind of have to know the commands in your head already,” Jones noted.

It has been revealed that that’s by design. From the start, the idea was to challenge people “either by confronting them with their past or demonstrating how difficult it was,” Jones said. His example: two friends, one with an Apple IIe and one with an IBM PC, whose computers “could never share” software. ICM continues that legacy, he said, “challenging the visitor to go beyond what they might feel comfortable with.”.

It has been revealed that volunteers have written cheat sheets to help newcomers, and Jones is encouraged when families come in and kids start typing BASIC programs. “That to me was the spirit of what PDP Planet and Living Computers was meant to be,” he mentioned.

Very little is behind glass. Jones jokes that a Timex Sinclair 1000, which would wipe your painstakingly typed program if you bumped it, is “the only computer that deserves to be behind glass.” The goal, he said, is to avoid “a boneyard that people walk through.”.

Other highlights include Galaxy Game, the first coin-operated video game, installed at Stanford in 1971 and now being restored, and a Thinking Machines CM-2 supercomputer, whose 40th anniversary ICM just celebrated with members of its original design team.

For younger engineers raised on modern tools, Jones has a go-to move. He asks if they’ve used Linux, then walks them over to the PDP-7, the type of machine Unix was first written on more than 50 years ago. Many of the basic commands they type every day started there.

That remote access helps explain why ICM has about 500 members and sponsors, even though only 81 members have visited in person this year. Memberships start at $36 a year. Along with a King County grant through 4Culture, they help cover rent, with personal funds from Jones filling the gap. The museum hopes to become self-sustaining within five years, and maybe someday buy its own building.

The museum’s name reflects the urgency. “We’re in this magic window right now, where the hardware can still run, we can still maintain it, you can replace parts,” Jones said. “But slowly we’re getting further and further away.”.

ICM is open Saturdays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission is $9 for adults and free for those under 18. Last May, the museum revived Vintage Computer Festival Pacific Northwest, which had been canceled in March 2020. The event drew 981 people, and it returns May 1–2 at the Tukwila Community Center.

Among the machines on the floor is MIT-AI, a DECsystem-2020 that once served as the ARPANET host for MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Lab. As Living Computers shut down in 2024, Christopher Zach, who sold the machine to Allen, told GeekWire he was ready to drive a U-Haul to Seattle to rescue it.

When a friend of Zach’s stopped by ICM’s booth at WorldCon and asked about “Chris’s computer,” Jones had a simple message to pass along: “Please just tell him it’s safe.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

According to recent reports, that detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain indicates nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's upcoming private AI app, ZetaLabs, releases alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

Industry observers note that the snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

According to recent reports, holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Recent findings suggest that two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the proposal, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain indicates it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain indicates the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

In a recent development, on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

According to recent reports, if it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Industry observers note that taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

Shares of Anthropic closed up 17% in first-day trading Thursday amid an otherwise down day for the broader market.

Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing.

Industry observers note that the offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

Sources indicate that for the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier initiative to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the manufacturer.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

According to recent reports, put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX, by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering.

The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books.

For the first nine months of the year, the manufacturer had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago.

Industry observers note that anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

According to recent reports, global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a major catch.

Industry observers note that drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to fresh data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

According to recent reports, sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how promptly the market is growing.

In a recent development, germany’s EV share topped 45% of latest car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of new car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

Recent findings suggest that north American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

Sources indicate that but here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of fresh energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

According to recent reports, those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Recent findings suggest that nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

According to recent reports, as the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 1:27 pmNovember 24, 2026 at 2:04 pm.

A billboard taking a swipe at Anthropic’s Claude might sound like the work of a rival AI manufacturer. This one is from the Seattle Art Museum.

“The only Claude you need is Monet,” the sign reads. It’s part of the latest wave of messages in SAM’s “Dear Seattle” campaign, which has spent the fall urging people to look up from their screens and see something in person.

Earlier billboards around the city told passersby to “come stare at something that isn’t your inbox” and noted that “even the algorithm thinks you should get out more.” The final batch pushes the AI jokes further, including one asking for “a little more art and a little less artificial” and another promising, “Your phone doesn’t have to know.”.

Tech billboards are a fixture in the San Francisco Bay Area, where AI startups cover Highway 101 and city streets with ads that often mean little to anyone outside the industry.

Sources indicate that they’re less common around Seattle. Anthropic put up a big orange Claude billboard over Aurora Avenue in 2024, and this spring Bellevue startup Summation put one up along SR 520 because “startup energy should be more visible around here,” its CEO told GeekWire.

In a recent development, “In a city where so much of our lives happens on screens, we’re making a playful case for the things you can only experience in person,” Kat Bryant Flaherty, SAM’s director of communications, said in a statement. She listed “the scale and texture of an artwork, a film with a room full of strangers, making something with your hands, or catching up with a friend over a meal.”.

The campaign is tied to changes at the downtown museum itself, where SAM is adding more public space and more reasons to linger, including hands-on art making and music in the Studio at SAM and the newly opened Bar Dojo restaurant.

The campaign runs through the end of the year, with more than 200 ads across the region — more than 20 billboards plus spots on light rail and digital kiosks.

SAM’s campaign is about the same size as the one Bellevue startup Statsig ran in the Bay Area in 2024, with more than 200 billboards and transit posters, but pointed in the opposite direction.

SAM is offering buy-one-get-one-free tickets in December with the code “LOVESAM,” good at both the downtown museum and the Seattle Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park, to encourage people to visit together.

“We’re hoping to grab attention, spark curiosity, and remind Seattle that there’s a lot happening at SAM worth leaving the house for,” Flaherty said.

The analyst suggested that the cryptocurrency may be approaching the lower end of its correction, even as selling pressure continues to weigh on its price.

“For me, $1 is roughly the bottom area for this cycle,” he stated.

While he described the $1 mark as the approximate bottoming zone for XRP during the ongoing cycle, he did not suggest that a definitive price floor had already been established.

His hesitation stems from the belief that investors will still have plenty of opportunities to accumulate alternative cryptocurrencies even after the broader market begins recovering. In his view, many altcoins could remain relatively cheap early in the next market rebound, meaning investors don’t necessarily need to rush into XRP before its downtrend runs its course.

“I’m not buying it yet,” he explained, making it clear that he would rather wait for a more favorable entry point than rush into the market.

XRP was trading at $0.9647 at the time of publication, down 2.3% over the previous 24 hours. The latest pullback followed a brief recovery to $1 on November 18, 2026, which proved short-lived as investors took profits, pushing the token back below the key psychological threshold.

It has been revealed that although VirtualBacon is not ready to accumulate XRP at current prices, he remains optimistic about its longer-term potential. The pundit believes the cryptocurrency could eventually reach $10, although he sees limited room for significant gains beyond that valuation.

In a recent development, the projected price target also highlights the scale of growth XRP would need. At $10 per token, its fully diluted valuation, calculated using the maximum supply of 100 billion XRP, would reach approximately $1 trillion.

Sources indicate that however, reaching such a valuation would require sustained demand, increased market participation, and significant capital flowing into the cryptocurrency. Notably, while VirtualBacon considers $10 achievable over the longer term, his outlook suggests that he sees this level as a more realistic upper target rather than expecting XRP to deliver substantially higher gains.

Industry News: Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Shows Us Why

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant.
  • According to recent reports, we have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model.
  • The SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value.

According to recent reports, we have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a company that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it.

The SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value.

This pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal.

The markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked.

In a recent development, when OpenAI launched ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025.

According to recent reports, the market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were unveiled later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal.

In a recent development, from there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year.

As an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others.

There were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when new technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole.

That is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April.

At my firm, Oxx, we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back.

In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike, whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October.

Industry observers note that the knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash.

Sources indicate that it produced the unintended consequence of driving firm ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value.

The panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private company transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this issue is to recognize there is actually a problem.

Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx, a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale.

Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
  • The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest.
  • Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he noted.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Firm Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Recent findings suggest that dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

In a recent development, the advertising sales team at media streaming tech giant Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski remarked Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”.

It has been revealed that replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding fresh features to existing platforms.

According to recent reports, kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Dreamteam also prepares to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

#99029. webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1069 w)

webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and claims it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • Sources indicate that A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and claims it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

Sources indicate that A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

Recent findings suggest that the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight customers want to hear.

Sources indicate that on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It notes TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Sources indicate that here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

In a recent development, none of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card indicates the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 fresh tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Industry observers note that anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card claims all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

According to recent reports, the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

Recent findings suggest that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting newly introduced models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine.
  • Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.
  • We first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company declared plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting newly introduced models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

We first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company declared plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

But don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a manufacturer with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

The UC3 originally launched in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t announced any intends to bring the UC3 to the United States.

And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

In much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

According to recent reports, I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

Recent findings suggest that I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost issue - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.
